questions.question: What must a function $\pi:A\to A$ do in order to be a permutation of $A$?
options: It must be strictly increasing.
It must be defined only on one element.
It must be bijective.
It must send $A$ into a larger set.
questions.explanation: A permutation of $A$ is a bijection from $A$ to itself. Injectivity prevents duplication and surjectivity prevents omission.

questions.question: What does a permutation do to the elements of a finite set?
options: It changes the size of the set.
It deletes one element and repeats another.
It sends every element to the same image.
It rearranges them without loss or duplication.
questions.explanation: Bijectivity assigns each original element to one distinct element of the same set, so a permutation only rearranges the elements.

questions.question: What happens when two permutations of the same set are composed?
options: The result is defined only for finite sets with two elements.
The result maps into a different set.
The result is again a permutation of that set.
The result is never bijective.
questions.explanation: The composition of two bijections $A\to A$ is again a bijection $A\to A$, so permutations are closed under composition.

questions.question: How many permutations does a finite set with $n$ elements have?
questions.explanation: There are $n$ choices for the first image, then $n-1$, down to $1$. The product is $n(n-1)\cdots1=n!$.

questions.explanation: A bijection pairs each output with exactly one input, so reversing every arrow defines another bijection $A\to A$, the inverse permutation.

questions.explanation: A fixed point is an element $a$ satisfying $\pi(a)=a$; the permutation leaves that particular element unchanged.
